## Overview & Summary


This blog post discusses the [Code
Review](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch09.html) chapter in the
[Software Engineering at Google book](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book).
The chapter explains why Google requires that someone other than the author
review every change before it enters the codebase. It describes the review
flow, the different kinds of approval a change may need, and the habits that
keep review fast, respectful, and useful.

## Introduction

Code review is far more than a bug-catching gate. At Google it is a way to
keep the codebase healthy over the long term and to spread knowledge across
teams. The chapter looks at the practical benefits (correctness,
comprehension, consistency) as well as the social ones, like shared ownership
and a historical record of why decisions were made.

### Code Review Flow

The typical flow is deliberately simple, and most changes follow the same
stages.

**What are the steps of the typical code review process at Google, and how
could they map onto our own projects?**

<details> <summary>Click to Expand for the Answer</summary>

1. The author creates a change and runs automated checks (tests, linters,
   static analysis) locally.
2. The author requests a review and describes what the change does and why.
3. Reviewers read the change and leave comments, from required fixes to
   optional suggestions.
4. The author modifies the change and replies to each comment, either by fixing
   the issue or by explaining a disagreement.
5. A reviewer gives an "LGTM" (looks good to me) once they are satisfied.
6. After all required approvals and passing checks, the change is committed.

</details>

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Create change] --> B[Request review]
    B --> C[Reviewer comments]
    C --> D[Author modifies & replies]
    D --> C
    D --> E[LGTM]
    E --> F[Commit]
```

Automation matters here too. Presubmit checks run before a human spends time
on the change, so reviewers can focus on design, clarity, and correctness
instead of formatting or trivially detectable problems.

## Why Review Code? The Benefits

### Code Correctness

A second pair of eyes catches logic errors, missed edge cases, and unclear
assumptions that the author is too close to see. Finding these problems before
they land is much cheaper than finding them in production.

### Code Comprehension

If a reviewer cannot understand a change, future maintainers probably cannot
either. Review works as an early readability test: a confusing change is a
signal to simplify the code or explain it better through naming, structure,
comments, or a clearer description.

**If a reviewer asks a question about your code, what does that tell you?**

<details> <summary>Click to Expand for the Answer</summary>

* the code (or its description) may not be clear enough on its own
* the fix is usually to improve the code or add documentation, not just to
  answer in the comment thread

</details>

### Code Consistency

Review enforces shared conventions so a large codebase feels like it was
written by one team. Consistent code lowers the cost of moving between projects
and of reading unfamiliar code, and it lets reviewers spend their attention on
substance instead of style.

### Psychological and Cultural Benefits

Knowing a colleague will read your work encourages care. Review also
normalizes giving and receiving feedback and builds a sense of shared
ownership. Done well, it reinforces teamwork rather than gatekeeping.

### Knowledge Sharing and Historical Record

Reviewers learn about parts of the system they do not own, and authors pick up
techniques and idioms from reviewers. The discussion attached to a change also
becomes documentation: months later it can explain *why* something was written
the way it was.

## Three Kinds of Approval

A single change at Google may need several distinct sign-offs, and one person
can sometimes provide more than one.

| Approval type | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Correctness and comprehension** | Is this change right, and can another engineer understand it? |
| **Ownership** | Does an owner of this part of the codebase agree it belongs here? |
| **Readability** | Does the code follow the language's idioms and the codebase's style? |

**Why might it help to separate these approvals instead of having one reviewer
judge everything?**

<details> <summary>Click to Expand for the Answer</summary>

* each reviewer can focus on one kind of judgment
* code owners protect their area without needing to review language style
* readability reviewers spread good language habits across the organization

</details>

## Code Review Best Practices

Review can introduce friction and delay if it is done poorly. A handful of
habits keep it worth the cost for both individuals and the organization.

**Discussion Question: Have we run into any of these problems with code review
as a group?**

### Be Polite and Professional

Review is a conversation between colleagues. Feedback should be about the code,
not the person, and should explain *why* a change is requested. Treat each
comment as a to-do item that deserves a response. If you disagree, explain your
side rather than silently marking the comment resolved, and consider asking the
reviewer to "please take another look" (PTAL).

Authors should remember that once code is committed it belongs to the team.
Be open to questions and ready to explain your choices.

### Write Small Changes

Small changes are easier to understand, faster to review, less likely to hide
bugs, and simpler to roll back. A rough rule of thumb from the chapter is that
a "small" change is around 200 lines or fewer. For larger features, break the
work into a sequence of independently reviewable steps.

### Write Good Change Descriptions

The first line works like an email subject: a short summary of the change.
The rest should explain what changed and why, with a list if there are many
modifications. Vague descriptions like "fix bug" or "updates" are discouraged,
since the description becomes part of the permanent record.

### Keep Reviewers to a Minimum

More reviewers do not automatically mean better review. Each additional
reviewer adds delay and can dilute responsibility, because everyone assumes
someone else looked carefully. Choose reviewers who cover the required
approvals, and if several are needed, have each focus on a different part of
the change.

### Automate Where Possible

Anything a machine can check reliably (formatting, linting, tests, common bug
patterns) should be checked by a machine. Presubmits save everyone time and
leave humans free for bigger issues with the code.

## Different Types of Code Reviews

As we read this section, consider which of these categories the code we write
as a class most often falls into.

### Greenfield Reviews and New Code

New code deserves the closest look at design: Is the API sensible? Is it well
tested? Will it be maintainable and fit within the larger system?

**Why might greenfield review be more common in our projects than at Google?**

<details> <summary>Click to Expand for the Answer</summary>

- our codebases are smaller
- our projects are newer

**And what else?**

**Finally, why do you think it is called "greenfield"?**

</details>

### Behavioral Changes, Improvements, and Optimizations

Here reviewers ask whether the change is really needed, whether it solves the
stated problem, and whether it risks breaking existing behavior. Remember that
some of the best changes are deletions.

### Bug Fixes and Rollbacks

A bug fix should address that bug and nothing else, and reviewers should check
that it targets the root cause. Rollbacks need to be reviewed quickly, so it is
wise to keep them in mind whenever you make a change.

### Refactorings and Large-Scale Changes (LSC)

Mostly mechanical edits can be reviewed with a different lens: confirm that the
transformation is consistent and behavior-preserving rather than scrutinizing
every line as new logic.

## Review Speed and Culture

Slow reviews are costly. Authors lose context, switch tasks, and are tempted to
batch more work into each change, which makes the next review even harder.
Small changes, automation, and a shared expectation of quick turnaround all
help. Just as important, review works best where people see it as a normal and
valued part of collaboration, not as an evaluation of their competence.

## Moving Forward

Many of these practices can be adopted on any team. Consider agreeing on a
review turnaround time, keeping pull requests small, writing descriptions that
explain the *why*, and moving style checks into continuous integration.

What aspects of code review do we do differently from Google? Are there
practices we should adopt that we are not currently using?

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" title="Open-Source Tool for Software Engineers" collapse="false"}

Our team built `CodeGuardian`, a lightweight, dependency-free Python
command-line tool that runs as a Git pre-commit hook to enforce code review
practices before changes are committed.

The tool checks staged files against `OWNERS` files to confirm that every
required owner has recorded an LGTM ("Looks Good To Me") approval, and that a
designated readability approver has signed off. It also warns about possible
duplicate function and class names and flags required review comments that have
gone unanswered for more than 24 hours. Errors block the commit, while warnings
are reported without blocking it.

You can view the project here: [CodeGuardian on
GitHub](https://github.com/Rivan-Deets/CodeGuardian).

:::
